messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: time-limited warmup & covar estimator accumulators
parts:
For estimating mass matrices for HMC and covar matrices
for Metropolis, we now use batches divided exponentially
like follows:

51--100, 101--200, 201--400, 401--800

I'm not sure what we do if the user specifies 735
warmup iterations. Mike had a suggestion to divide
it as 735/2^N.

But what do we do with adaptation for a fixed time?
Then we don't know the magic number 735 ahead of time.

One solution would be to just two accumulators.
There's a current accumulator. It starts accumulating
sufficient stats at iteration 51. At iteration 101,
the accumulator is made the old accumulator and a new
one is started. At iteration 200, the current accumulator
is made the old one and a new one's started and so on.

Then if we stop short, we can just add the old and current
accumulators for the final result.

We could even add the accumulators as we went if the
solver's not too expensive.

We could even use the pair of accumulators to turn off
adaptation early if the mass matrix estimated for the previous
batch is similar to that for the current batch. Of course,
that only checks that mass matrix estimation has stabilized,
not that we've reached the typical set.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] time-limited warmup & covar estimator accumulators
parts:
Ok, maybe there's an obvious answer to this, but is there a particular
reason we're doing a batched estimator like this? Strictly speaking
we don't even need to stop after the "warmup" period, as you can
continue the covariance estimation indefinitely so long as it
converges. (in the sense of diminishing adaptation, see Jeff
Rosenthals work.) It seems like that would be the simplest approach.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] time-limited warmup & covar estimator accumulators
parts:
On 4/29/13 1:37 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> Ok, maybe there's an obvious answer to this, but is there a particular
> reason we're doing a batched estimator like this? Strictly speaking
> we don't even need to stop after the "warmup" period, as you can
> continue the covariance estimation indefinitely so long as it
> converges. (in the sense of diminishing adaptation, see Jeff
> Rosenthals work.) It seems like that would be the simplest approach.

I suggested the reverse -- downweighting old samples rather
than downweighting new samples. Here's my message and Michael B's
reply:

I wrote:
> Can we do something like a moving average type adaptation where
> old information dies out in strength over time? Then there'd be
> no discretization of the epochs for training covariance during
> warmup.
>
> I'd think it'd be easy to add to Welford's algorithm by adjusting
> the ratio in the updates to do some past discounting.

Michael B replied:
Technically that's not hard to do. I think the problem with a moving average is that it can still be too sensitive to
the past. In particular, convergence of the Markov chain (and, perhaps more importantly, the disparity in values
between unconverted and converged) can often outpace the forgetfulness of the moving average estimator. Isn't that why
we went to sequential windows in the first place?
-------------

- Bob

On Mon, Apr 29, 2013 at 1:52 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> On 4/29/13 1:37 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
>>
>> Ok, maybe there's an obvious answer to this, but is there a particular
>> reason we're doing a batched estimator like this? Strictly speaking
>> we don't even need to stop after the "warmup" period, as you can
>> continue the covariance estimation indefinitely so long as it
>> converges. (in the sense of diminishing adaptation, see Jeff
>> Rosenthals work.) It seems like that would be the simplest approach.
>
>
> I suggested the reverse -- downweighting old samples rather
> than downweighting new samples.

Actually "diminishing adaption" would be achieved by simply weighting
all samples equally, as the adaption of the resulting proposal
distribution would diminish over time as the estimate of the
covariance matrix converged. Downweighting of older samples may
violate diminishing adaption, I haven't checked thoroughly.

I guess the point here is that I don't fully understand the nature of
the adaption we're trying to do here. There is a (relatively)
standard adaptive form of (Gauss) Metropolis which is something like:

1) Compute sample covariance S of all previous iterations.
2) Use covariance matrix S to construct proposal distribution, e.g.,
p(x_t+1 | x_t, S) = N(x_t+1 | x_t, c S).
3) Use proposal distribution with Metropolis-Hastings accept-reject decision.

I've used this with relatively good success on problems where the
gradients were not available. It's actually really easy to implement
and, with a few variations (regularize the estimate of S using a Inv
Wishart prior, use a mixture model with a "small variance" proposal
component, etc), can be made extremely robust.

It sounds like we're trying to do something very different though.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] time-limited warmup & covar estimator accumulators
parts:
> For estimating mass matrices for HMC and covar matrices
> for Metropolis, we now use batches divided exponentially
> like follows:
>
> 51--100, 101--200, 201--400, 401--800
>
> I'm not sure what we do if the user specifies 735
> warmup iterations. Mike had a suggestion to divide
> it as 735/2^N.
Actually with the push I made yesterday the last batch "snaps" to the total number of warm-up samples.

> But what do we do with adaptation for a fixed time?
> Then we don't know the magic number 735 ahead of time.

I think the more fundamental issue is given a fixed time how do we figure out how to split the time between warmup and sampling. Once we have a criterion for such a splitting incorporating adaptation shouldn't be too hard. Not to say that I have any idea what a good criterion would be (yesterday I was throwing around time/sample estimation to convert the fixed time into fixed samples and appeal to our usual approach).

> Ok, maybe there's an obvious answer to this, but is there a particular
> reason we're doing a batched estimator like this? Strictly speaking
> we don't even need to stop after the "warmup" period, as you can
> continue the covariance estimation indefinitely so long as it
> converges. (in the sense of diminishing adaptation, see Jeff
> Rosenthals work.) It seems like that would be the simplest approach.

I'm just using this particular batch approach for historical reasons, but we definitely need some form of forgetting.

The problem is that we're adapting to a moving target: the current state of the Markov chain. If we just used a diminishing estimator the result would be highly biased by the initial samples which are likely to be drawn far from the typical set. Because we only adapt during warmup we don't need to appeal to Rosenthal's work, but we could always add diminishing adaptation if it were so desired provided it's paired with some form of forgetting.

Now the easiest form of a forgetful adaptation would be a moving average, but I fear that HMC would force the vulnerabilities of a moving average. The problem is that often HMC converges really, really fast and only the first few samples are outside of the typical set. Those samples are really far outside the typical set, however, and effectively serve as outliers that pull the expectations further than they should. Having a batch after which no previous samples are used helps to mitigate such outliers.

This all suggest a more robust warm-up procedure. Because we don't want to adapt until we've hit the typical set (or are at least close to it), we could run a unit-metric trajectory a few times to deal with approximate convergence, then introduce an adaptive stage that handles learning the metric as well as finishing the convergence. We could also abandon HMC considerations and use funkier trajectories (apply the NUTS criterion without a binary tree, for example, or terminate trajectories once they start regaining energy). We've discussed it before and I have some ideas, but haven't had any chance to play with them given all of the refactoring for R-HMC.

> all samples equally, as the adaption of the resulting proposal

> covariance matrix converged. Downweighting of older samples may
> violate diminishing adaption, I haven't checked thoroughly.

> I guess the point here is that I don't fully understand the nature of
> the adaption we're trying to do here. There is a (relatively)
> standard adaptive form of (Gauss) Metropolis which is something like:
>
> 1) Compute sample covariance S of all previous iterations.
> 2) Use covariance matrix S to construct proposal distribution, e.g.,
> p(x_t+1 | x_t, S) = N(x_t+1 | x_t, c S).
> 3) Use proposal distribution with Metropolis-Hastings accept-reject decision.
>
> I've used this with relatively good success on problems where the
> gradients were not available. It's actually really easy to implement
> and, with a few variations (regularize the estimate of S using a Inv
> Wishart prior, use a mixture model with a "small variance" proposal
> component, etc), can be made extremely robust.
>
> It sounds like we're trying to do something very different though.

Pretty sure that scheme breaks detailed balance. it might work in Gaussian-like cases where the covariance is approximately constant, but when the covariance varies with position the proposals won't be balanced. Rosenthal showed that you can adapt and converge asymptotically provided that the adaption diminishes (a la Robbins-Monroe). Again, consider the case where of spatially-varying curvature: the adaptation won't have a single fixed point but many so that the adaptation oscillates and you don't get asymptotic detailed balance.

So if it stops at 735, which samples are in the
estimate of covariance?

I wouldn't worry about optimally balancing time split
between adaptation and sampling --- we can just go with 50-50
for now. The optimal time balance will depend on
the problem, because we only want to warmup as long as we
need to in order to get to the typical set and get a decent
estimate of covariance in the samples.

And thanks for all the other clarifications!

Marcus -- this is for both estimating a covariance matrix
for Metropolis and for estimating an (inverse) mass matrix
for HMC/NUTS.

If we use a Robbins-Monro-like weighting scheme on the
samples, we could keep going with adaptation, right? Not
that there seems to be much point in doing that versus what
we're doing.

If covariance varies across the posterior, there isn't even
a "right" global covariance matrix to use for Metropolis proposals
(or for HMC mass matrices).

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] time-limited warmup & covar estimator accumulators
parts:
The method outlined above is effectively the "Adaptive Metropolis"
described by Roberts and Rosenthal in section 2 of
http://probability.ca/jeff/ftpdir/adaptex.pdf

The question is what you actually expect the sampler to adapt to?
With a windowed, moving or discounted estimate you'll get local
estimates of curvature, but you'll always have to stop the adaption
before you can draw any real samples. Then the question is what
covariance estimate do you use for the non-warmup samples? The last
window which is only good locally or a global estimate? Local
estimates will be strongly stuck in a single region and give highly
confident but potentially inaccurate estimates.

I would suggest that with most methods (excluding things like RMHMC)
the only thing you can hope for is to adapt to the global covariance
structure, in which case you might as well continue adapting
indefinitely (or until it's numerically converged). Early iterations
can be ignored, but in my experience their impact tends to be
relatively quickly forgotten.

That said, different approaches may be called for between HMC and Metropolis.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] time-limited warmup & covar estimator accumulators
parts:
> So if it stops at 735, which samples are in the
> estimate of covariance?

As it stands, when the 100-200 window terminates the 200-400 window is created. At that time the algorithm "peeks" into the next window, 400-800, sees that it passes the 735 total, and then expands the window to fill, leaving a 200-735 window. Shrinking the 400-800 window would also work, but yields a much smaller window susceptible to higher estimation noise.

> I wouldn't worry about optimally balancing time split
> between adaptation and sampling --- we can just go with 50-50
> for now. The optimal time balance will depend on
> the problem, because we only want to warmup as long as we
> need to in order to get to the typical set and get a decent
> estimate of covariance in the samples.
50/50 time split would be easy, I'd just worry about performance when someone runs a complex model for only a few minutes. In any case, it's definitely an active research area.

>
> 50/50 time split would be easy, I'd just worry about performance when someone runs a complex model for only a few minutes. In any case, it's definitely an active research area.

Andrew's motivation here is just to be able to control runs
by time instead of iterations. His plan all along was to just
look at R-hat (n_eff), and if it's too large (small), run
again for longer time. No way we can guarantee convergence
if someone specifies 2 seconds (or 2 hours, depending on the
model) as the allotted run time. It'll just save us from having
to interrupt a running process (or thread in the case of R) if
it goes too long.

- Bob

The simplest idea was to specify time t.
Warmup, terminating with the first iteration ending after
time t/2. Then sample, terminating after time t.

There was some discussion about whether to have a minimum
number of samples (split-R-hat needs at least 4, I think,
to avoid a zero in denominator of the variance estimate).

I don't know that there's any deeper motivation for
Andrew wanting to split time and number of samples other
than it bounds the time (or iterations) wasted adapting
after convergence during warmup.

R-hat's easy enough to do online, but split R-hat isn't.
But you could do it in batches.

We could also specify running for a max of time t and a max
of K iterations. That would terminate warmup after K/2
iterations if it occurs before t/2 and terminate sampling
after K total iterations if it occurs before time t.

- Bob
